questions.q: When does the block of an if statement run?
questions.explain: The condition does not have to be a boolean. JavaScript converts it with the truthy and falsy rules, so if ("hello") runs and if (0) does not.
options: Only when the condition is exactly true

questions.q: An if has an else. How many of the two blocks run?
questions.explain: With if … else, exactly one block runs: the if block when the condition is truthy, otherwise the else block.
options: Both, first the if block, then the else block
Both, but only when the condition is truthy

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 0 is falsy, so if (count) is false and the else block runs. Here that is what you want, but say it on purpose: if (count > 0). When 0 is a valid value that must not count as missing, check for "missing" explicitly instead, for example count !== undefined.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A string with a space is not empty, so it is truthy and if (title) passes. Trimming it gives "", so the second check catches it. That is why the lesson checks title.trim() === "".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The title is not empty, so the if block is skipped. The line after the block is not part of the if, so it always runs.
options:
A task needs a title
This line always runs

questions.q: In an if statement, what marks the block of code that belongs to it?
questions.explain: The condition goes in parentheses and the code to run goes between { and }. Indenting by two spaces does not change the meaning; it helps people see what belongs to the if.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 30 is not below 0 and not below 24, but it is below 168 (24 * 7). Only the first matching branch runs, so else is skipped.

questions.q: The conditions are in the wrong order. What does this print?
questions.explain: 95 is at least 50, so the first branch runs and the rest are skipped. "Excellent" can never print. Put the most specific condition (score >= 90) first.

questions.q: In a chain of else if branches, several conditions can be true. Which rule does the lesson give?
questions.explain: Conditions are tested from top to bottom, and the first truthy one wins. A general condition at the top would hide the more specific ones below it.
options: JavaScript runs every branch whose condition is true
Only the first true branch runs, so put the most specific conditions first
JavaScript runs the last true branch, so put the most general condition last
The order does not matter because else catches the rest

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The outer condition loggedIn is false, so the inner if is never reached, even though the role is "admin". The outer else runs.
options:
Show the admin panel
Show the login page

questions.q: Your function has four levels of nested if blocks. What does the lesson suggest?
questions.explain: One level of nesting is fine, but three or four are hard to follow. Guard clauses check each bad case on its own line and return, so the code stays flat.
options: Nothing, deep nesting is the clearest style
Flatten it with guard clauses that return early for the bad cases
Turn every if into a nested ternary
Replace the if blocks with switch and no break

questions.q: What does condition ? a : b give?
questions.explain: The ternary operator takes three parts: a condition, the value for truthy, and the value for falsy. It chooses between two values.
options: a when the condition is falsy, b otherwise
a when the condition is truthy, b otherwise
Always a, and b is a fallback for errors

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: count === 1 is false, so the ternary gives "tasks". Only exactly 1 uses the singular.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: done is false, so the ternary gives the second value, a single space.

questions.q: When is a ternary the right tool?
questions.explain: Use a ternary to pick one of two values. For longer logic, or for choices that do things, use if. Never nest ternaries; they become unreadable.
options: For any decision, because it is shorter than if
For a short choice between two values
For choices that print, save or delete things
For three or more choices, by nesting ternaries

questions.q: How does switch compare the value with each case?
questions.explain: switch uses strict equality. The string "200" and the number 200 are different types, so they do not match.
options: It only compares the first letter of strings
It checks whether the value is truthy

questions.q: What does default do in a switch?
questions.explain: default is the catch-all branch. Use it to handle unknown values, for example by printing Unknown status.
options: It sets a default value for the variable
It runs when no case matches, like else

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two cases with nothing between them share the same code. "review" matches, runs the shared line, and break leaves the switch.
options:
Someone is working on it
Finished

questions.q: This switch has no break. What does it print?
questions.explain: Without break, JavaScript "falls through" and runs the code of every case below the match. Here it is on purpose; most of the time it is a bug.
options:
page the on-call engineer
write to the error log
write to the normal log

page the on-call engineer
write to the error log

questions.q: The programmer forgot one break. What does this print?
questions.explain: The "editor" case has no break, so it falls through into the "viewer" case. That case has a break, so default does not run.
options:
can edit
can read
no access

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: switch compares with ===. The string "404" is not the number 404, so it falls to default.

questions.q: Inside a function, the cases of a switch use return instead of break. Is that correct?
questions.explain: return ends the function straight away, so nothing after it runs. No break is needed.
options: Yes: return ends the whole function, so it also leaves the switch
No: every case still needs break after the return
No: you cannot use return inside a switch
Yes, but only in the default case

questions.q: You let one case fall through into the next on purpose. What should you do?
questions.explain: Most fall through is a bug, so readers will assume yours is one too. A short comment tells them it is on purpose.
options: Nothing, fall through is always expected
Add a comment saying the fall through is deliberate
Write the case values in alphabetical order

questions.q: When is switch clearer than a chain of else if?
questions.explain: switch fits one value with many exact options, like a status name. For ranges or different variables, use if and else if.
options: When each branch tests a different variable
When you compare one value against many fixed options
When you want loose comparison with ==

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: return ends the function straight away. For -1 the guard returns before the console.log. For 2 the guard is skipped and both lines run.

questions.q: What is a guard clause?
questions.explain: A guard clause checks one bad case at the top of a function and returns early. The happy path is then the last line, and the code stays flat.
options: A comment that explains why a check is needed
An early check of a bad case that leaves the function with return
An else block at the end of a chain

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first guard that matches wins. User 2 does not own the task, so the second guard returns. User 1 owns it, but it is locked, so the third guard returns.
options:
no: not your task
no: task is locked

no: task is locked
no: task is locked

no: not logged in
no: task is locked

questions.q: You write a function that decides whether a user may delete a task. Which design is safest?
questions.explain: For permissions, always fail closed: start from "no" and allow only after every check passed. If a check is missing or confused, the answer is still "no".
options: Return "yes" at the top, then return "no" if you find a problem
Check every rule first and return "yes" only as the last line, after all checks passed
Return "yes" when you are not sure, so users are not blocked
Skip the checks when the user is logged in

questions.q: When may you leave out the braces, as in if (!user) return "no";?
questions.explain: A block with one statement can skip its braces. The lesson keeps this for one-line guards, so it is always clear what the if controls.
options: When the block is a single statement; keep it for one-line guards
Whenever the block has fewer than five lines

questions.q: In the age check, why does the empty string need its own guard?
questions.explain: Number("") is 0, a real number. Without the guard, an empty form would pass the number checks and say "rejected: too young" instead of "age is required".
options: Because Number("") is 0, so an empty form would be treated as age 0
Because Number("") is NaN, which crashes the program
Because trim() does not work on empty strings

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "abc" becomes NaN and "17.5" becomes 17.5; neither is a whole number. Number ignores the spaces around " 13 ", so it gives 13. One check rejects both text and decimals.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 13 is not below 13 but is below 18, so it needs consent. 18 is not below 18, so it is allowed. Spaces trim to "", which the guard catches before any number check.
options:
allowed with parental consent
allowed
invalid: age is required

rejected: too young
allowed
invalid: age is required

allowed with parental consent
allowed with parental consent
rejected: too young

allowed with parental consent
allowed
rejected: too young

questions.q: Why does the lesson test the ages 12, 13, 17 and 18 on purpose?
questions.explain: Boundary values sit right next to each rule's limit. If a comparison is off by one, only an edge value shows it.
options: Because they are the most common ages of users
Because bugs hide at the edges, like writing < where you meant <=
Because tests only need four values

questions.q: A value comes from a form, typed by a stranger. What should your function do first?
questions.explain: Outside input can be anything: empty, text, a decimal, a huge number. Throw out every bad input first; then the decision part is short and safe.
options: Use it straight away; the form already checked it
Validate it with guard clauses, then make the decision
Convert it with Number() and trust the result
Wrap the decision in a ternary

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every comparison with NaN is false, even <=. So !(total > 0) is a handy guard: it is true for negatives, zero and NaN.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each guard returns, so later checks do not need an upper limit. 79 fails >= 80 but passes >= 70, and 69 reaches the last line.

questions.q: The shipping(total, country) exercise starts with if (typeof total !== "number" || !(total > 0)) return "invalid total";. Which input does this guard not reject?
questions.explain: "80" is a string, so typeof rejects it. NaN and -5 fail total > 0. Only a positive number like 20 gets through.

questions.q: Finish sign with if, else if and else: return "negative" below 0, "zero" for 0 and "positive" above 0. The program should print negative zero positive.
questions.explain: Test the conditions from top to bottom. Only the first true branch runs, and else catches the rest.

questions.q: Finish grade with guard clauses: "A" for 90 and above, "B" for 80 to 89, "C" for 70 to 79 and "F" below 70. The program should print A A B C F.
questions.explain: Check the highest grade first. Because each guard returns, score >= 80 only runs when you already know the score is below 90.

questions.q: Finish statusText with a switch: return "OK" for 200, "Created" for 201, "Not Found" for 404 and "Unknown" for anything else. The program should print OK | Created | Not Found | Unknown.
questions.explain: Each case returns, so no break is needed. The string "200" does not match the number 200, because switch uses ===, so it goes to default.

questions.q: Finish shipping(total, country) with guard clauses. Return "invalid total" when total is not a positive number (this includes strings and NaN). Orders of 50 or more ship for 0. Otherwise shipping is 5 for "NG" and 15 elsewhere.
questions.explain: Reject bad input first: typeof catches strings, and !(total > 0) catches negatives, zero and NaN. Then a ternary picks between two prices.
questions.expected:
0 5 15
invalid total invalid total invalid total

questions.q: Finish taskLabel with a ternary so it returns "1 task" for 1 and "N tasks" for any other number. The program should print 0 tasks | 1 task | 5 tasks.
questions.explain: A ternary is ideal for choosing between two values. Only exactly 1 uses the singular; 0 uses the plural.

questions.q: Finish checkAge. The input arrives as text. Return "invalid" when it is empty (after trimming), not a whole number, or outside 0 to 130. Otherwise return "too young" under 13, "consent" for 13 to 17, and "allowed" for 18 and older.
questions.explain: Validate first: reject empty text (because Number("") is 0), then non-integers, then the range. After that the decision is three short lines.
questions.expected:
allowed allowed consent consent too young
invalid invalid invalid invalid invalid

questions.q: Finish canDelete(user, task) with guard clauses, failing closed. Return "no: not logged in" when there is no user, "no: not your task" when task.ownerId is not user.id and the user is not an admin (user.role === "admin"), and "yes" only at the end.
questions.explain: Check the bad cases first and return early. "yes" is the last line, so it is only reached after every check passed.
questions.expected:
no: not logged in
no: not your task
yes
yes

questions.q: Finish priorityIcon with a switch. "high" and "urgent" both return "!!" (share one case body), "normal" returns "!", and anything else returns "-". The program should print !! !! ! -.
questions.explain: Two cases with nothing between them share the same code. default catches every other value.

questions.q: Finish dueLabel(hoursLeft) with an else if chain: "Overdue" below 0, "Due today" below 24, "Due this week" below 168, and "Due later" otherwise. The program should print Overdue | Due today | Due this week | Due later.
questions.explain: Test the smallest range first. 24 is not below 24, so it is "Due this week"; 168 is not below 168, so it is "Due later". The edges show whether you used < correctly.
questions.expected: Overdue | Due today | Due this week | Due later

questions.q: Finish welcome(user). With no user (null), return "Please log in". For a user with role "admin", return "Admin: NAME". For anyone else, return "Hello, NAME". Use the user's name.
questions.explain: Guard against the missing user first; otherwise user.role would throw on null. Then one check for the special case, and the normal case last.
questions.expected:
Please log in
Admin: Ada
Hello, Grace
